title: Partial hydatidiform mole: fetal tissue + focal trophoblast + mixed villi (triploid)
vignette: A 16-year-old girl comes to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was 12 weeks ago. She is sexually active and does not use contraception. The patient had a miscarriage last year that required a dilation and curettage. Urine pregnancy test is positive. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an intrauterine gestational sac without fetal cardiac activity, and a dilation and curettage is performed. Pathology shows fetal tissue, focal trophoblastic hyperplasia, and some enlarged villi interspersed with normal villi. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

clues.text: miscarriage last year that required a dilation and curettage
clues.note: Prior miscarriage (and extremes of maternal age) are risk factors for a molar pregnancy.
The presence of FETAL tissue distinguishes a PARTIAL mole (fetal parts present) from a complete mole (no fetal tissue).
FOCAL (patchy) trophoblastic proliferation is characteristic of a partial mole (complete moles show diffuse hyperplasia).

clues.text: some enlarged villi interspersed with normal villi
clues.note: A MIX of enlarged (hydropic) villi with normal-appearing villi is typical of a partial mole (complete moles have diffusely enlarged villi).

whatMatters: Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy with pathology showing FETAL TISSUE + FOCAL trophoblastic hyperplasia + SOME enlarged villi mixed with normal villi = PARTIAL hydatidiform mole (triploid, 69,XXX or XXY). Answer E. (A complete mole has NO fetal tissue, diffuse hyperplasia, and diffusely enlarged villi.)
strategy: Use the triad to separate partial from complete mole: partial = fetal tissue present + FOCAL hyperplasia + SOME villi enlarged (mixed), triploid. Complete = no fetal tissue + DIFFUSE hyperplasia + all villi enlarged, 46,XX (paternal). Reject miscarriage (normal villi, low hCG, no trophoblastic hyperplasia), and the malignant GTDs: invasive mole (villi invading myometrium), choriocarcinoma (sheets of anaplastic trophoblast, NO villi, lung mets), and placental site trophoblastic tumor (intermediate trophoblast, human placental lactogen).

eliminations.label: Choriocarcinoma - malignant, no villi
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a malignant gestational trophoblastic disease with sheets of anaplastic cyto- and syncytiotrophoblasts and NO chorionic villi; often presents with bleeding and lung metastases. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this specimen has villi and fetal tissue (not anaplastic villous-free trophoblast). ✅ Correct if: villous-free anaplastic trophoblast with metastases.

eliminations.label: Complete mole - no fetal tissue, diffuse changes
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a benign mole with DIFFUSELY hydropic villi and DIFFUSE trophoblastic hyperplasia, 46,XX (all paternal), and NO fetal tissue. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this case HAS fetal tissue, FOCAL hyperplasia, and a MIX of villi - features of a PARTIAL mole. ✅ Correct if: no fetal tissue, diffuse villous edema, 'snowstorm' ultrasound, markedly high hCG.

eliminations.label: Invasive mole - villi invading myometrium (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a mole (usually complete) that invades the myometrium; diagnosed by histologic evidence of villi INVADING muscle (often on hysterectomy). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this curettage shows fetal tissue and mixed villi WITHOUT documented myometrial invasion - a partial mole, not invasion. ✅ Correct if: molar villi invading the myometrium.

eliminations.label: Miscarriage - normal villi, no trophoblastic hyperplasia
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a pregnancy loss before 20 weeks with fetal tissue but NORMAL villi and trophoblast and a low/appropriate hCG. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this pathology shows trophoblastic HYPERPLASIA and enlarged hydropic villi - abnormal features of a partial mole, not a simple miscarriage. ✅ Correct if: fetal loss with normal villi and no trophoblastic proliferation.

eliminations.label: Placental site trophoblastic tumor - intermediate trophoblast
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a rare malignant GTD of INTERMEDIATE trophoblast that produces human placental lactogen. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it lacks villi and the mixed hydropic/normal villous pattern seen here. ✅ Correct if: intermediate trophoblast proliferation secreting human placental lactogen.

reasoning: Early-pregnancy bleeding + curettage pathology with fetal tissue
Plus FOCAL trophoblastic hyperplasia and SOME enlarged villi mixed with normal villi
This triad defines a partial hydatidiform mole (triploid 69,XXX or XXY)
mechanism: Hydatidiform moles are benign gestational trophoblastic diseases arising from aberrant fertilization with over-representation of PATERNAL genes, producing abnormal trophoblastic proliferation and elevated beta-hCG. A PARTIAL mole is TRIPLOID (69,XXX or 69,XXY) - typically from fertilization of a normal egg by two sperm - so it contains both maternal and paternal DNA. Because maternal DNA is present, FETAL tissue/parts can form, and the histology shows FOCAL trophoblastic hyperplasia with SOME hydropic (enlarged) villi INTERSPERSED with normal-appearing villi - exactly this specimen. It often presents like a missed abortion (early bleeding, no fetal cardiac activity). In contrast, a COMPLETE mole is 46,XX (entirely paternal), has NO fetal tissue, shows DIFFUSE trophoblastic hyperplasia and DIFFUSELY hydropic villi, a 'snowstorm' ultrasound, and markedly elevated hCG (with risk of theca-lutein cysts, hyperemesis, early preeclampsia). Prior miscarriage and extremes of maternal age are risk factors. The malignant GTDs differ histologically: invasive mole (villi invading myometrium), choriocarcinoma (anaplastic trophoblast, no villi, hematogenous lung spread), and placental site trophoblastic tumor (intermediate trophoblast, human placental lactogen).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Repro/Path > partial mole: triploid (69,XXX/XXY), fetal tissue present, FOCAL trophoblastic hyperplasia, SOME enlarged villi; complete mole: 46,XX paternal, no fetal tissue, diffuse changes, snowstorm, very high hCG.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Fetal tissue + focal hyperplasia + mixed villi = PARTIAL mole (not complete/invasive).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on hydatidiform mole, triploid, trophoblastic hyperplasia, hydropic villi, or gestational trophoblastic disease? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Complete mole = no fetal tissue/diffuse; invasive mole = myometrial invasion; choriocarcinoma = no villi; miscarriage = normal villi; PSTT = intermediate trophoblast.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: partial mole = triploid, fetal tissue + focal hyperplasia + mixed villi; complete mole = 46,XX, no fetus, diffuse, snowstorm, high hCG.

keywords.front: Fetal tissue + focal trophoblastic hyperplasia + mixed villi

keywords.back: 46,XX (paternal); no fetal tissue; diffuse hyperplasia; snowstorm; very high hCG

keywords.front: Partial vs complete mole - fetal tissue

keywords.back: Anaplastic trophoblast, NO villi; lung metastases

firstAid.detail: Repro: triploid; fetal tissue + focal trophoblastic hyperplasia + some enlarged villi.
Path > complete mole, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, PSTT.
Repro > ↑beta-hCG; complete = 'snowstorm'/no fetus; partial = fetal parts.

memoryHook: Partial mole = a triploid 'part-baby, part-mole': fetal tissue with a patchy mix of swollen and normal villi; the complete mole is all mole, no fetus.
